old_title: Man City 'found guilty of almost all Premier League charges' in bombshell verdict
new_title: Man City chairman insists innocence despite reports on guilty verdict

A verdict over Premier League charges against Manchester City is finally set to be delivered after a bombshell report said the club have been "found guilty on almost all of the charges".
The Independent understands that the former champions have been found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018, in what would be a seminal moment for the richest football league in the world.
The landmark ruling, first reported by The Athletic, follows one of the most significant court cases in the history of sport, with the verdict also having major repercussions for City's rivals. The Premier League have declined to comment, however.
City, currently top of the Premier League after five games, were charged with over 115 alleged breaches of the Premier League's financial rules in February 2023, with the club always denying any wrongdoing throughout the process.
An independent commission was appointed following a four-year investigation. Sanctions have not yet been decided, according to The Athletic, and City are expected to appeal. A club spokesperson said the Premier League process "remains ongoing".
City have been England's most successful team since the club's fortunes were transformed by Sheikh Mansour's takeover in 2008. There are a wide range of punishments available to the top-flight's authorities. Sanctions could include fines and/or points deductions, and even expulsion as a member of the Premier League.
Follow all the latest news, reaction and analysis to one of the most important moments in the Premier League's history:
Man City are expected to appeal - what does that look like?
Now, the club will have the chance to appeal against the decision of one of the most significant court cases in the history of sport.
Regardless of the judgement, both sides - the Premier League and Manchester City - knew they would have the chance to appeal within 14 days of the ruling.
Such an appeal would trigger a fresh three-person commission to look into the case, the members of which will be selected by Murray Rosen KC, the chair of the Premier League's judicial panel.
This would lead to a further delay of the imposition of any sanctions or points deductions until the appeal process is complete.
A Manchester City spokesperson said: "The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC's position remains consistent with the club's statement of February 2023.
"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair minded regulator, free from partisan influence."
Simon Jordan reacts to reported verdict on Man City charges
Former Crystal Palace owner Simon Jordan has commented on Man City's 115 charges: "If you can expel Southampton from the worlds richest game
"What can you do to a club, found guilty of a breaching financial regulations on a systemic level in the worlds richest league?
"The length and breadth of this and who this touches is going to be so revealing."
Man City timeline: From Abu Dhabi takeover to 115 Premier League charges
So how did we get here? It's coming up on two decades since a takeover that changed English football - this is the full timeline:
Could the Independent Football Regulator play a role?
If City are indeed found guilty of the most serious charges, the Independent Football Regulator could push for the removal of key figures. That body does have powers under section 34.
Some in football are even broaching the idea of a forced sale due to the severity of the case, given that this would be perceived as the greatest case of cheating in English football history.
It should not be forgotten that this is ultimately about the allegation of submitting false accounting.
The charges didn't just involve accusations of breaching financial regulations on several occasions, but of not providing accurate payment details.
A sanctions hearing would determine the most immediate punishments. Multiple sources feel this can't possibly go without a huge points deduction, particularly given the recent precedent of Everton and Nottingham Forest, potentially enough to relegate the club.
Prime Minister warns not to 'jump to conclusions' after report of verdict
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned people should not "jump to conclusions" on City, when asked whether they should be stripped of their Premier League titles.
He told ITV Granada Reports: "I've only just been made aware of it - I think these are reports at this stage. But if they're confirmed, obviously I will want to look at the report of the independent commission.
"People shouldn't jump to those kind of conclusions (about City having their titles taken off them). I know, this has been a long process between the club and the Premier League. I think quite a contested process. So I don't think it's as simple as jumping to conclusions.
"I think we would all need to study the independent commission's report in some considerable detail before reaching any conclusions."
WATCH: Fans react as Manchester City reportedly found guilty
Verdict could 'open floodgates' to legal challenge, expert says
A guilty verdict against Manchester City for a mass breach of Premier League rules would "open the floodgates" to further cases against them, a legal expert has said.
The club are reported to have been found guilty on virtually all the charges laid against them by the Premier League back in February 2023, charges the club have always strenuously denied.
The Premier League has not commented on the reports, while a spokesperson for City said the process remained ongoing "with significant elements to be completed".
An appeal by City in the event of a guilty verdict would be a certainty, but if the independent commission's reported decision is upheld, Paul Stothard, a partner at global law firm Norton Rose Fullbright, felt the ramifications would be seismic.
"This result, if upheld, will open the floodgates to further legal challenges," Stothard said.
"Manchester City being found liable for 114 out of 115 rule breaches means that other clubs may choose to pursue compensation for lost revenue, missed European qualification or relegation - though they would need to be able to prove how City's breaches impacted on their own ability to compete and their quantifiable loss.
"The outcome underscores the need for regulatory mechanisms in professional football and, moving forward, could help reshape how football governance balances commercial interests with the principles of fair play in what is now a multi-billion-pound competition."
The Man City verdict is an earthquake - what comes next could be even bigger
After a seismic day for football, Miguel Delaney explains why many more tremors could be to come:
City odds to be relegated slashed with Arsenal now heavy favourites to win Premier League
Man City have been priced at just 9/2 to be relegated following the reports that they have been found guilty of almost all of their 115 financial charges.
Enzo Maresca's side are top of the Premier League by three points after five games and were very narrow second favourites (6/5) behind Arsenal (11/10).
But now City are 5/2 to win the league, with Arsenal just 8/11.
What happened when Man City were punished by Uefa?
The Premier League's case against Manchester City is not the first time the club have been involved in a long-running legal drama.
In November 2018, German newspaper Der Spiegel publish leaked documents, obtained by Football Leaks, alleging Manchester City had inflated the value of sponsorship deals in order to circumvent FFP rules.
Uefa launched investigation into Manchester City over alleged breach of FFP and in February 2020, announced a two-year Champions League ban and €30m fine. They ruled City committed "serious breaches" of FFP regulations between 2012 and 2016.
City describe the process as "prejudicial" appealed to The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), who overturned City's two-year Champions League ban and reduced their fine to €10m.
Cas ruled that City were cleared of "disguising equity funds as sponsorship contributions" but added the club did "fail to cooperate with Uefa authorities".

Follow all the latest news, reaction and analysis to one of the most important moments in the Premier League's history:
Manchester City chairman releases statement after reports say club are guilty of breaching financial rules
Khaldoon Al Mubarak addressed supporters in a letter maintaining the club's innocent despite reports claiming they will be found guilty of 114 charges against them.
What are the Premier League's charges against Man City?
The hearing into Manchester City's alleged 115 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules has reached its long-awaited verdict, with City set to found guilty of all except one charge.
The champions were referred to an independent commission in February 2023 following a four-year investigation. The Premier League said the alleged breaches took place over a nine-season period, from 2009 to 2018, and relate to providing accurate financial information.
Can Man City appeal against verdict on Premier League's charges?
Manchester City have been found guilty by an independent commission over the club's 115 breaches of the Premier League's financial rules, according to The Athletic.
City insist the process "remains ongoing" surrounding the charges relating to providing accurate financial information and failing to comply with Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) over a nine-year period, between 2009 and 2018.
Could Manchester City be expelled from the Premier League over financial breaches?
Manchester City are set to be found guilty of 114 of the 115 charges made by the Premier League, in a seismic moment for English football.
An independent commission is poised to announce the results of its four-year investigation into the case, according to The Athletic. No sanctions have yet been decided, but City are expected to appeal against the ruling.
What were Man City's 115 Premier League charges?
Manchester City's charges concerning breaking financial fair play rules surround a nine-year period, from 2009 to 2018.
They were also charged with failing to co-operate with Premier League investigations concerning the club's finances.
Initially charged in 2023, the club was accused of:
- Failure to provide accurate and up-to-date financial information (2009-2018): 54
- Failure to provide accurate financial reports for player and manager compensation (2009-2018): 14
- Failure to comply with UEFA's regulations, including Financial Fair Play Regulations: 5
- Breaching Premier League Profitability and Sustainability regulations (2015-2018): 7
- Failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations (2018-2023): 35
What has Enzo Maresca said on Man City's charges?
Manchester City manager Enzo Maresca, who took over from Pep Guardiola in the summer, said before the start of the season that he had "no concerns" over the Premier League charges.
Maresca was previously Guardiola's assistant and was at the club in February 2023 when they were charged by the Premier League with breaking their financial rules.
"The only thing I can say is three years ago, the treble season, I was here, and it was the same words about this," Maresca said in July.
"In three years, it's still the same. Nothing has happened. I don't have any concerns, personally."
Maresca has won his first five games of the Premier League season after signing a three-year contract.
No sanctions have been announced and Man City are expected to appeal
Manchester City insist the process "remains ongoing".
The Premier League have not yet announced sanctions, but City are expected to appeal the long-awaited verdict after they were found "guilty on almost all of the charges".
Possible sanctions include fines, points deductions, and even expulsion from the Premier League.
Those sanctions could be applied now, or retrospectively. That could mean City are stripped of titles and trophies.
City insisted in February 2023 that they were "surprised" by the charges and said there was evidence to prove their innocence.
How did we get here?
The landmark ruling follows one of the most significant court cases in the history of sport. City were charged with over 115 alleged breaches of the Premier League's financial rules in February 2023 following a four-year investigation.
The Premier League said the alleged breaches took place between 2009 and 2018, and related to providing accurate financial information and failing to comply with profit and sustainability rules (PSR). Other charges included an accusation of failing to co-operate with the Premier League's investigation, which was prompted by the Football Leaks revelations.
City have been England's most successful team since the club's fortunes were transformed by Sheikh Mansour's takeover in 2008. The club won the Premier League three times between 2009 and 2018, a period in which the club also won one FA Cup and three League Cups.
Under former manager Pep Guardiola, City won the Premier League in 2019, 2021, 2022, 2023 and 2024, including an unprecedented run of four in a row. In 2023, the club also won the Champions League for the first time, completing a historic 'Treble' of major prizes.
Man City 'found guilty of almost all Premier League charges'
Yesterday The Athletic's David Ornstein has reported that Manchester City "have been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges".
We still await confirmation of this from the Premier League with the verdict into the charges still to be officially revealed.
Such an overwhelming verdict would represent victory for the Premier League, who charged City in February 2023.
Why was verdict delayed?
The independent hearing into Man City's charges concluded in December 2024, yet the nature of the case was described as "hugely complex," leading to a lengthy delay in the verdict.
The timeframe between the start of the hearing and the judgement has stretched to almost three years.
Premier League chief executive Richard Masters admitted to Sky Sports before the 2025/26 season that he had grown frustrated with the situation.
"It's an independent judiciary essentially," he said. "They are then in charge of the process and its timings. They hear the case, they decide the outcome and we have no influence over it or its timing.
"My frustration is irrelevant really, I just have to wait. Legal processes rarely take less time than you anticipated. But we have to be patient."
